short: CSL is the DNA-binding transcription factor at the end of the Notch pathway, named for its three orthologues: CBF1/RBPJ in mammals, Suppressor of Hairless in Drosophila and LAG-1 in C. elegans. Humans have one broadly expressed gene, RBPJ, plus the pancreas-restricted paralogue RBPJL. RBPJ binds the seven-base element GTGGGAA, often written on the other strand as TTCCCAC, and does so whether or not Notch is active: without a Notch intracellular domain it recruits corepressors, and with one it assembles an activating ternary complex with Mastermind-like coactivators. Some Notch targets carry two sites in a head-to-head pair with fixed spacing, an SPS, which allows two Notch complexes to dimerize. Notch signaling through RBPJ controls lateral inhibition, T-cell specification and vascular development, and is constitutively activated in T-cell acute lymphoblastic leukemia.
long:
## The factors

There is essentially one CSL protein per genome. In humans the gene is RBPJ (older names RBP-J,
RBPSUH, CBF1); the paralogue RBPJL (RBPSUHL) is restricted to pancreatic acinar cells, where it
replaces RBPJ in the PTF1 complex. RBPJ is expressed in nearly every tissue. It is not a
Notch-specific protein in the sense of being present only when Notch is: RBPJ is constitutive,
and Notch activation changes what RBPJ does rather than whether it exists. The DNA-binding
module has three parts: an N-terminal domain with a Rel-homology-like fold, a beta-trefoil
domain (BTD) and a C-terminal domain. The crystal structure of CSL on DNA showed that the
Rel-like domain and the BTD grip the site from opposite faces, with the BTD doing double duty as
the docking site for the RAM peptide of the Notch intracellular domain (NICD). On Notch
activation, NICD binds RBPJ and recruits a Mastermind-like coactivator (MAML1-3) to form the
ternary complex; in the absence of NICD, RBPJ binds corepressors such as SPEN/SHARP and
associated histone deacetylases and demethylases. So the same protein on the same sequence can
repress or activate.

## The motif

The literature consensus is GTGGGAA, usually written with a 5' pyrimidine as YGTGGGAA, and its
reverse-strand form is TTCCCAC. Only about six or seven positions carry information, and the
models in these databases are short accordingly: the representative motif here is TTCCCA, which
is simply the reverse complement of TGGGAA with the 5' GT trimmed off, and JASPAR's RBPJ matrix
(TGGGAA) is the same element on the forward strand. The GGG at the center is the least tolerant
part of the site. Only one symbol, RBPJ, appears across all four databases, so there is no
paralogue problem inside the family, and the four models agree closely (cohesion 0.93). The
difficulty is external. TGGGAA and its complement TTCCCA sit inside the purine-rich sequence
space used by ETS cores (GGAA), NFAT (GGAAA) and the half-sites of NF-kB and STAT models, and
the label-agreement statistics for all four RBPJ motifs are low (0.3) precisely because their
nearest neighbours across the four databases frequently belong to those families. A separate
feature is site architecture rather than sequence: some Notch-responsive promoters carry two
CSL sites in head-to-head orientation with a spacer of roughly 15-17 bp, the Su(H)-paired site
or SPS, first described in the Drosophila Enhancer of split complex. The spacing and orientation
matter because they allow the ankyrin repeat domains of two Notch molecules to contact each
other across the DNA, which sharpens the response. No PWM captures an SPS; you have to look for
two matches at the right distance and orientation.

## Where it acts

RBPJ sites are found in both promoters and enhancers, and the best-studied targets are the HES
and HEY families (HES1, HES5, HEY1, HEY2), DTX1, NRARP, and, in lymphoid cells, PTCRA, IL2RA and
MYC. Genome-wide, RBPJ and Notch1 occupy thousands of sites, and occupancy is dynamic: in
Drosophila, Su(H) binding at target enhancers is transient and only partly overlaps its
Notch-independent binding, and in mammalian cells RBPJ occupancy at many sites increases on
Notch activation rather than being fixed. Conversely, a subset of sites is occupied by CSL
without Notch and functions in default repression, keeping targets off in cells that have not
received a signal. RBPJ co-occurs with lineage factors that determine which of its sites are
used: TCF/LEF and GATA3 in T cells, ETS and RUNX factors at lymphoid enhancers, and PTF1A
through RBPJL in pancreas.

## Biology and disease

Rbpj-null mouse embryos die around embryonic day 10 with defects in somitogenesis and
vasculature, phenocopying loss of Notch1 more closely than any single ligand mutant. Through
Notch, RBPJ drives lateral inhibition in neurogenesis, T-cell versus B-cell specification,
arterial-venous specification and intestinal secretory-versus-absorptive choice. Activating
NOTCH1 mutations that stabilize NICD are the commonest genetic lesion in T-cell acute
lymphoblastic leukemia, and the resulting Notch1/RBPJ complexes bind a largely conserved set of
enhancers in human and mouse leukemia cells. Notch loss of function causes disease as well:
NOTCH3 in CADASIL, JAG1 and NOTCH2 in Alagille syndrome, and inactivating NOTCH1 mutations in
squamous carcinomas, where the pathway is tumor-suppressive. RBPJ itself is mutated in Adams-Oliver
syndrome.

## Reading a hit

The important caution is interpretive, not statistical: a match to the RBPJ motif, and even
measured RBPJ occupancy, does not mean Notch signaling is active at that site. RBPJ binds
constitutively and represses in the unsignaled state, so the sequence marks a potential Notch
response element, not a signaled one. To claim active signaling you need evidence for NICD or
MAML at the site, or a change in output on gamma-secretase inhibition. The site is also short:
six or seven informative bases occur often by chance, and the purine-rich core is easily
confused with ETS, NFAT or NF-kB half-sites, which is what the low label-agreement scores in
these data reflect. Two matches in head-to-head orientation about 15-17 bp apart are much
stronger evidence than one.
caveats: One factor, RBPJ, so a hit does not have a paralogue problem inside the family; the risk is outside it. The informative core is only six or seven bases and overlaps ETS, NFAT and NF-kB purine-rich half-sites, which is why all four RBPJ models here score low label agreement against the other databases. The HOCOMOCO model (SUH.H14CORE.0.P.B) is ChIP-derived, so it reports where RBPJ was found, not what RBPJ binds in isolation. Most importantly, RBPJ occupies sites constitutively and represses without Notch, so neither a sequence match nor a ChIP peak licenses the conclusion that Notch signaling is active.
